anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: The approved L1 anchor has a small four-target 3D isometric scene, but its visible solution still requires viewpoint/ray reasoning, ordered mining prerequisites, hazard and support checks, and exact canvas targeting. Crackglaze L1 removes that 3D viewpoint and motor-control burden, yet adds a stateful orthogonal route, a learned two-colour fuse mapping, and failure on expired revisits. The comparison supports Crackglaze's low profile as a compact but non-static task, rather than treating its L1 label as proof that it is a one-click task.

evidence.explanation: The approved anchor is L1 with four exposed targets, one lava block, one fragile support, and no sealed targets.
The anchor generator builds depth-sorted voxel faces, target blockers, and click-ray prerequisites rather than a flat independent target list.
The visible anchor binds canvas rotation/mining and gives the simplified mode separate controls while retaining canvas target selection.
The anchor grader independently checks rotation/input source, raycast identity, prerequisites, hazards, durability, and extracted targets.
Crackglaze replay and assignment make the route depend on fuse ages and deliberately fail geometry-only alternatives.

anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: The approved L2 task searches one field for one target: cursor motion reveals convergence, decoys create false responses, and one click within the accepted radius completes it. Its target does not alter the field or create a later decision. Every accepted Crackglaze move advances previously lit fuses and can change which future route is safe, so even the compact profiles have more dependent temporal planning than this L2 anchor.

evidence.explanation: The approved L2 configuration uses two decoys, 26 noise stars, a 112-pixel reveal radius, and one 28-pixel accepted click radius.
The anchor generator creates one target, decoys, structured stars, and noise on a fixed surface and stores one expected click.
The visible anchor responds to pointer distance and then accepts a target click; its simplified branch enters coordinates and selects once.
The anchor grader checks the selected point against one target radius and mode-specific input source, with no multi-step world replay.
Crackglaze advances the step and ages all lit tiles on each accepted movement, including movements whose destination then expires.

anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: Both baselines are approved L3 but stress different demands. Gyroscopic Tilt Board has continuous analog tilt, momentum, collision/well avoidance, and three ordered lamps before a cup. Crackglaze has much less continuous motor control and no physics, but requires visible colour discrimination, retained fuse age, and route choices on a changing floor with two obscured revisits. That is a plausible same-level cognitive/control balance, while not evidence that the two tasks have equal empirical difficulty.

evidence.explanation: The approved L3 anchor has three ordered lamps, three walls, three wells, faster dynamics, and full analog-drag input.
The anchor generator and physics state include walls, hazards, waypoint order, momentum, friction, collision, and control/tick parameters.
The visible anchor advances physics ticks from tilt input and uses separate compass-button and analog-drag surfaces.
The anchor grader replays deterministic physics and checks ordered lamps, hazards, cup placement, and mode-specific control source.
Crackglaze's dependent burden is discrete fuse-age replay and deliberately selected route discrimination rather than continuous dynamics.

anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: The approved L4 task is an 18-by-11 warehouse with five ordered gates. Each move changes a hidden die orientation, and only four sparse scanners reveal it; the grader replays the exact route and face conditions. Crackglaze L4 is a smaller 2D graph with four visible glaze classes and four hidden revisit cells, so it has comparable state-dependent route risk but less long-horizon orientation bookkeeping and no roll physics. This places Crackglaze L4 above the current L3 anchor in route/memory breadth but below or around the lower edge of this L4 anchor.

evidence.explanation: The approved L4 anchor specifies five barriers/gates, an 18-by-11 board, four sparse scanners, and initial-plus-scanner orientation visibility.
The anchor search state includes both warehouse position and die orientation.

The anchor grader replays orientation, scanner visibility, gate faces, barriers, and the complete route.
Crackglaze L4 increases to four glaze/fuse classes, four hidden revisits, a seven-column core, and subtle contrast but retains three lanterns and discrete movement.

anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: The approved L5 task requires four exact-score swaps on a changing board. Every valid swap resolves matches, collapses/refills candies, changes the next board, and must satisfy an exact total and wave constraints. Crackglaze L5 also has dependent decisions rather than merely a long walk: four lantern placements, four shuffled fuse classes, and six hidden revisit states constrain route order. It is nevertheless a simpler discrete graph replay than the Candy L5 changing-board search, so it fits within the highest named profile without proving equality to that anchor.

visible_baseline_solution: A screenshot-only player receives the task rules and one post-action frame at a time. The rendered board shows a sparse orthogonal ceramic floor, distinct glaze colours, the start marker, lantern markers, the door, the current walker, and visible lit/hairline/crazed/critical or fallen-tile appearances. The generated calibration corridor is the only route from the start area into the generated core, and its witness tiles expose the shuffled colour-to-fuse mapping when the player watches their stages. The player must then use the visible adjacency geometry, the learned mapping, and a remembered ledger of when previously left tiles were lit to choose a route that collects every lantern and reaches the exit before any required revisit has expired. At difficulty 3, two revisited core tiles are under the gallery treatment, so their crack strokes are not directly available; the route must retain their age information across later decisions. A move into a shattered destination fails, submits the transcript, and receives a fresh challenge; reaching the exit before collecting all lanterns does not pass. Full mode requires clicking the intended tile, while Simplified mode requests the same adjacent move with a stationary arrow button. There is no wall-clock fuse progression in the supplied configuration: state changes on movement actions and each observation contains one frame.

baseline_judgment.rationale: The current L3 label fits the intended problem as a source-based placement. It is materially more dependent than Cursor-Controlled Constellation Hunt L2 because every move ages prior state and route choices can invalidate later revisits. It is less demanding than Blind Dice Courier L4 because it has a smaller 2D floor, no hidden orientation/roll dynamics, and only three lanterns at baseline. It is comparable in broad cognitive burden to Gyroscopic Tilt Board L3, trading continuous momentum control for fuse-mapping and hidden-age planning. It remains below the changing-board exact-score search in Exact-Change Candy Cascade L5. This is an intended-level judgment, not empirical human or agent calibration.

evidence.explanation: The current baseline is explicitly the L3 profile: a 5-by-6 core with 15 cells, three lanterns and glaze classes, two gallery cells, standard contrast, and three fuse lengths.

Fuse age changes the rendered tile stage, while the same colour and tile metadata are shown in both interaction branches.
Each movement updates lit ages, records success or expiry, collects lanterns, and only completes at the exit after all lanterns are collected.
The independent grader replays the same age and expiration rule and rejects a forged movement outcome.

uncertainties: No human or computer-use-agent calibration was run in this audit, so the absolute boundary between the broad L3 and L4 labels is not measured.
The full-mode coordinate-frame mismatch in finding CG-001 can add an unintended hit-location burden; its practical failure rate needs the parent's isolated runtime check.
The gallery overlay suppresses crack strokes but leaves stage-dependent ceramic styling in the CSS; whether that is perceptually recoverable from screenshots needs a rendered check.

The source has no explicit one-way calibration phase flag. The calibration path is nevertheless structurally placed between the start and core, so this review did not treat backtracking within that corridor as a proven shortcut.

findings.claim: Full-mode click coordinates are recorded in a rendered-board bounding box that includes CSS padding and grid gaps, while the grader checks them against ideal equal-cell rectangles with a small tolerance. A normal click at the center of an outer rendered tile can therefore be rejected even though it visibly targets that tile.
findings.causal_explanation: The browser computes pointInBoard from getBoundingClientRect of .crack-board. The CSS gives that element 18px padding, nonzero grid gaps, and a perspective transform. The grader's _cell_rect instead starts each cell at column/columns and row/rows with no padding or gap term, and the full branch rejects points outside that ideal rectangle. The actual tile and accepted point regions may overlap, so this is not source-proven to make the task impossible, but it imposes an unintended edge-biased precision requirement and breaks clean Full/Simplified tolerance equivalence.

evidence.explanation: Full-mode event points are normalized using the complete .crack-board getBoundingClientRect.
The measured board has a fixed width/height, 18px padding, grid gaps, and a perspective transform.
The grader constructs ideal unpadded cell rectangles and allows only a .008 normalized tolerance.
Full transcripts must provide a tile_click point inside those grader rectangles; simplified transcripts have no point requirement.

findings.recommended_action: Align the full-mode recorded point and grader rectangle to the same rendered content/target coordinate frame, or grade the actual clicked tile element; then add isolated clicks at centers and edges of generated tiles before treating the interaction pair as equivalent.

findings.claim: Gallery cells hide the crack strokes but still receive stage-specific brightness, saturation, and transform rules, so their age stage may remain indirectly visible rather than fully hidden.
findings.causal_explanation: The task says darkened tiles' crack stages cannot be seen. The browser derives stage from fuse age and adds stage-hairline/crazed/critical classes. The CSS applies visible filter and transform changes to .ceramic for those classes, while the under-gallery rule only forces the two crack elements' opacity to zero; the gallery shadow overlays the tile but does not remove those stage rules. Whether the remaining cues are reliably recoverable from a screenshot is a rendering question, but the source does not implement complete stage isolation.

evidence.explanation: The task describes darkened tiles whose crack stages cannot be seen.
Tile stage is computed from the hidden age/fuse ledger and attached as a class before the gallery class.
Hairline, crazed, critical, and shattered stages change ceramic brightness/saturation/transform or disappearance.
The under-gallery rule hides only crack-a/crack-b and adds an overlay; it does not cancel stage-specific ceramic styling.

findings.recommended_action: Render representative hidden tiles and determine whether age stages are actually distinguishable. If the intended information is hidden, suppress all stage-dependent visible cues inside the gallery treatment; otherwise revise the task/profile rationale to describe the indirect cue.

concise_summary: The intended Crackglaze Crossing ladder is source-supported: L1 is a compact two-colour stateful route, L2 adds topology and a third mapping class, L3 adds hidden revisit ages, L4 adds a fourth class and weaker/more numerous hidden states, and L5 adds a collect-all dependency and six hidden revisits. The current L3/full baseline is a plausible intended placement between the approved L3 and L4 anchors, with no historical pre-control implementation to preserve. However, Full and Simplified are not fully equivalent in the source: full click points use a padded/gapped rendered frame while grading uses ideal cell rectangles, and the gallery treatment may leak stage through ceramic filters/transforms. These require parent runtime checks or profile/input revision.
limitations: This is source analysis only; no browser, generation sweep, grader run, exported-verifier run, human calibration, or computer-use evaluation was performed.
No historical pre-control implementation is supplied, so only current default versus explicit L3 baseline equivalence is supported.
The minimum_policy_failures field is active in world selection but is not a direct runtime quota; it was not counted as independent difficulty.
Generated topology, lantern placement, route length, and fuse-to-colour shuffle vary by seed, so exact burden is not established by one source configuration.
No source-supported indistinguishable adjacent pair or unused difficulty parameter was found beyond the two implementation caveats recorded above.
